_readme: Content for the body map and indicator panels. 'nasa' statements are paraphrased from the NASA page named in 'source' and must be shown with that link. 'team' statements are the team's own rationale and must never be attributed to NASA. 'reviewStatus' is internal and is not rendered. A human on the team must check every 'nasa' statement against its source page before submission.

hazards.title: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight (NASA Human Research Program)

hazards.name: Space Radiation

nasa.text: NASA's Human Research Program describes space radiation as one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight.

A higher risk of cancer and of degenerative diseases such as heart disease and cataracts has been observed in radiation-exposed populations on Earth. For astronauts the main concern is the long-term impact, which depends on the total dose and how quickly it is received.

hazards.reviewStatus: drafted from source, needs human check

hazards.name: Isolation and Confinement

nasa.text: Crews live isolated and confined in a small space for long periods, and NASA studies the behavioral responses this produces.
Altered light and dark cycles, a small and noisy habitat, and stress can disrupt circadian rhythms, and morale and motivation can change as a mission unfolds.

hazards.reviewStatus: drafted from source, needs human check

hazards.name: Distance from Earth

nasa.text: The farther a crew travels, the harder it becomes to receive instructions, supplies, and medical care from Earth.
At Mars, communication can be delayed by up to 20 minutes each way, so crews must be able to handle problems without real-time help from mission control.

hazards.reviewStatus: drafted from source, needs human check

hazards.name: Gravity Fields

nasa.text: Muscles, bones, the inner ear, and organs all have to adjust each time the crew moves to a different level of gravity.
In weightlessness, body fluids shift toward the head, and without countermeasures astronauts lose bone and muscle.

hazards.reviewStatus: drafted from source, needs human check

hazards.name: Hostile/Closed Environments

nasa.text: A spacecraft is a closed ecosystem. Temperature, pressure, lighting, noise, microbes, and the crew's immune responses all have to be monitored.
In spaceflight, stress hormone levels rise and the immune system is altered, which could make crew members more susceptible to allergies or illness.

regions.label: Brain and behavior

nasa.text: Circadian rhythms can be disrupted by altered light and dark cycles, a small and noisy habitat, and stress. On Mars, the day is about 37 minutes longer than on Earth.
Morale and motivation can change as a mission unfolds, and more restricted, less connected environments are associated with a higher likelihood of behavioral, cognitive, or psychiatric conditions.
NASA countermeasures include tracking sleep and activity with actigraphy, LED lighting tuned to support circadian rhythms, a short self-test of vigilance and attention, and journaling.

regions.team: Sleep hours and a one-tap mood rating are the two signals a crew member can log every day without equipment. Several low days in a row are a reason to talk to the crew or the ground, before performance is affected.
regions.reviewStatus: drafted from source, needs human check

regions.label: Heart and circulation

nasa.text: In weightlessness, fluids move toward the head. This may put pressure on the eyes and affect vision.
After spaceflight, some astronauts cannot maintain their blood pressure when they stand up, which can lead to lightheadedness and fainting. Some decline in heart function has also been noted.
A higher risk of degenerative diseases, including heart disease, has been observed in radiation-exposed populations on Earth.
NASA countermeasures include aerobic and resistive exercise, fluid monitoring, and thigh compression cuffs. A lower-body negative pressure device is being considered.

regions.team: Blood pressure and resting heart rate are quick to measure and show how the cardiovascular system is coping with fluid shifts and with the exercise program. A trend matters more than one reading.
regions.reviewStatus: drafted from source, needs human check

regions.label: Metabolism and nutrition

nasa.text: On a mission far from Earth there is no resupply. The crew carries all of its food, equipment, and medical supplies, and NASA researches how to keep food and medication usable for the whole mission.
Researchers analyze astronauts' urine for kidney stone risk and adjust diet, exercise, and water intake to prevent it.

regions.team: Blood glucose is a simple, self-measured marker of how diet and routine are affecting a crew member. We track it as a nutrition signal. The sources above do not state that spaceflight changes blood glucose, and this app does not claim that it does.
regions.reviewStatus: drafted from source, needs human check

regions.label: Immune system and body temperature

nasa.text: In spaceflight, stress hormone levels rise and the immune system is altered, which could increase susceptibility to allergies or illness.
Microbes change in space, and microbes that live on people spread more easily from person to person in a closed habitat.
NASA countermeasures include air quality monitoring, thermal control of the habitat, blood and saliva analysis, testing for reactivated latent viruses, and regular cleaning and microbial sampling.

regions.team: Body temperature is the simplest early sign of infection. In a closed habitat with an altered immune system, a fever is worth reporting early.
regions.reviewStatus: drafted from source, needs human check

regions.label: Bones and muscles

nasa.text: In spaceflight, weight-bearing bones lose on average 1% to 1.5% of their mineral density per month.
Muscle is lost faster in microgravity without proper diet and exercise, and bone loss raises calcium excretion, which together with dehydration can increase the risk of kidney stones.
NASA countermeasures include aerobic and resistive exercise, bisphosphonates for bone loss, potassium citrate (under study) for kidney stone risk, and imaging of muscle and bone.

regions.team: Bone and muscle loss cannot be self-measured with a simple daily reading, so this region is information only. It is here because it is the reason the daily exercise routine matters.

regions.label: Radiation exposure

nasa.text: A higher risk of cancer and of degenerative diseases such as heart disease and cataracts has been observed in radiation-exposed populations on Earth. The main concern for astronauts is the long-term impact.
Missions to the Moon and Mars will last much longer than a typical six-month stay on the space station, so the total radiation received, and the associated risk, may be higher.
NASA countermeasures include shielding, radiation monitoring, and operational procedures.

regions.team: This panel shows radiation dose rates measured by instruments aboard the International Space Station and on other spacecraft from low Earth orbit to the surface of Mars, from NASA's RadLab database, and recent solar events from NASA's DONKI space weather database. The cumulative dose shown is an illustration for the mission day, not a personal dose record.

nasa.text: At Mars, communication can be delayed by up to 20 minutes each way, so crews must be able to solve problems without real-time help from mission control.
NASA prepares crews for this with medical training, crew-performed ultrasound scans, onboard lab testing, and research into clinical decision support tools.

escalation.team: This is why the app gives self-care steps first and tells the crew member when a result should go to the Crew Medical Officer or the flight surgeon.
